extracted.intended_audience: British colonial administrators, missionaries, traders, tropical medical practitioners, and general readers interested in West African policy and health
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and critique concerning missionary activity, colonial trade and administration, technical education, and prevention/treatment of tropical disease (especially malaria) in West Africa. The text mixes policy recommendations for officials and practical survival/medical advice for residents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of technical mission-schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Any technical school is better than none, and apart from lay considerations, is of great religious value to the mission indirectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industrial mission-schools employ and occupy the lower faculties of natives, helping spiritual development and preventing boredom and moral decline among converts; technical schools are generally preferable to purely academic or parochial instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach trades actually wanted by the local economy
rubrics_metrics.description: In the majority of these crafts such as bookbinding, printing, tailoring, etc., are being taught which are not at present wanted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical instruction should be tailored to market demand and local requirements (i.e., agriculture, plantation work, sustainably usable trades) rather than importing European crafts that have little local demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume African intellectual incapacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The attempt to make out that the African is a child-form, 'an arrested development,' is not supported by facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies and educational programs should not be based on physiognomic or craniological claims (brain-weight, suture-closure) as evidence of incapacity; observational evidence supports adult learning and development when properly managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misdirected missionary effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Misdirected missionary effort has an evil effect on the native mind and has in many cases done harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missionary work should avoid imposing unsuitable European cultural forms (e.g., excessive schooling that causes physical harm, forced European dress) and instead emphasize practical technical instruction that benefits converts materially and morally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize harmful government over-regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Government does nearly as much [harm] ... tendency to get everything into the hands of a Council, or an Office, to be everlastingly nagging and legislating and inspecting, matters little; the result is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive administrative restrictions and protectionist measures (e.g., heavy restraints on trade or import duties) discourage commercial expansion and the ability of English traders to hold markets; permit freer trade to foster development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain and expand trade and plantations for native welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: The development of trade is a necessary condition for the existence of the natives ... the discovery of products in the forests ... and the making of plantations ... will give him a safer future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government and private initiatives should promote plantation agriculture and expanded interior trade to provide stable livelihoods and replace exhaustible bush-extraction economies; without trade expansion, native welfare will worsen despite other administrative improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent wasteful harvesting; implement sustainable cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Owing to the wasteful methods employed in its collection [rubber] it gets stamped out of districts ... when he has cleared the districts reachable by him, the trade is finished there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage sustainable harvesting methods and the establishment of cultivated sources (plantations) for key exports (rubber, palm oil) to avoid local depletion and collapse of the trade on which natives depend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate liquor sensibly rather than prohibit or over-tax
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not deny that the liquor traffic requires regulation, but it requires more regulation in Europe than it does in Africa ... all that is wanted is that the spirit sent in should be wholesome, and not sold at a strength over 45 degrees below proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid short-sighted measures like high import dues that kill legitimate trade; focus on ensuring the quality and appropriate strength of spirits and target restrictions to places with clear local alcohol-related problems (large coast towns) rather than blanket prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should be practical and adapted to local conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: What he wants teaching is how to work ... a thorough grounding in technical culture, suited to the requirements of their country, instead of the ruinous instruction they have been given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize vocational/technical education matched to local economic and climatic conditions; avoid overloading children with inappropriate 'headwork' in broiling schoolrooms or forcing European dress that harms health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic respect for indigenous social institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Both polygamy and slavery are, for divers reasons, essential to the well-being of Africa--at any rate for those vast regions of it which are agricultural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues caution about imposing European social norms universally; reformers should consider local social-economic roles of institutions before enforcing abrupt changes that could be harmful or impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize laboratory research to find better antimalarials
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who will make West Africa pay will be the scientific man who gives us something more powerful against malaria than quinine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fund and support laboratory investigators working on malaria; clinicians in the field can supply valuable material but concentrated lab work at home is needed to discover superior treatments/preventives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use microscopic blood examination to guide prognosis and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The German doctors make a practice of making microscopic examinations of the blood ... from these investigations they are able to judge fairly accurately how many remissions may be expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blood microscopy can indicate stage and severity of malarial infections and inform treatment timing, particularly because quinine affects the parasite in specific stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise caution with quinine in haematuric (haematuria) fever
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Plehn asserts ... that quinine has a very bad influence when the characteristic symptoms have declared themselves, and that it should not be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is conflicting clinical opinion: some practitioners (e.g., Plehn) report success by avoiding quinine in haematuric cases, whereas French heavy-dosing policies show high mortality; clinicians should weigh local evidence and proceed cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal preventive measures against malaria
rubrics_metrics.description: The best ways of avoiding the danger of the night air are--to have your evening meal about 6.30 or 7, --sleep under a mosquito curtain whether there are mosquitoes in your district or not, and have a meal before starting out in the morning, a good hot cup of tea or coffee ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recommendations include early evening meals (6:30–7:00), sleeping under mosquito nets regardless of apparent mosquito presence, taking a hot morning meal/tea before exposure, avoiding chill and excessive exertion where possible; many popular remedies (smoke-lamps, respirators, avoiding night air entirely) are impractical or ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate, properly timed alcohol as a protective stimulant
rubrics_metrics.description: All the evidence is in favour of alcohol, of a proper sort, taken at proper times, and in proper quantities, being extremely valuable. Mr. Stanley says that wine is the best form of stimulant, but that it should not be taken before the evening meal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alcohol (especially wine) in moderation and at appropriate times may help tolerance of the climate; regional differences exist (e.g., beer in Cameroon associated with higher haematuric fever incidence), so prefer wine and avoid alcohol before the evening meal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain drinking-water and washing-water sanitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The drinking and washing water of West Africa is liable to contain dermazoic and entozoic organisms ... nearly certain to import Trichocephalus dispar, Ascaris lumbricoides, Oxyuris vermicularis, and eight varieties of nematodes ... and, lastly, a peculiar abomination, a Filaria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure safe water supplies and hygiene to prevent a range of skin and helminth infections (tinea variants, intestinal nematodes, filaria); water safety is one of the few avoidable malaria/parasite-related risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select personnel adapted to the climate
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little doubt that a certain make of man has the best chance of surviving the Coast climate--an energetic, spare, nervous but light-hearted creature ... The full-blooded, corpulent and vigorous should avoid West Africa like the plague.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit or send individuals with constitution and temperament likely to tolerate tropics (lean, energetic, light-hearted) rather than those with corpulent, heavy constitutions; personnel selection affects mortality and operational success.
